```{r}
#| include: false
source("../../../book/R/setup.R")
```

A team with a Python person, an R person and someone writing a dashboard in
JavaScript has three plotting libraries, three sets of defaults, and no way to
put two of their figures on the same page without one looking wrong.

GOG tries the opposite arrangement. Instead of one plotting library per
language, there is one graphics engine, written in Rust, with four thin language
bindings sitting on top of it. Describe a plot in any of them and you get the
same picture: not a similar one, not one that needs its theme adjusted to match,
but the identical file.

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + color(continent)
```

## The shape of it

When you make a plot here, you are not drawing it. You are describing it. You
name a table, a shape to draw, and which column goes to which part of the
picture. Your language turns that into a short block of text and hands it over.
Something else reads the text and draws the picture.

That block of text has a name. It is the plot's **specification**, and building
one is the whole job of each of the four packages. They are specification
builders. Nothing else about them has to match, because nothing else about them
affects the picture.

![](../../images/pipeline.svg){fig-alt="Four language bindings, one for R, Python, Julia and
JavaScript, each build the same specification. It travels as JSON on standard
input to gog-cli, the bridge, then to gog-core, the engine, which draws the
SVG."}

Read the diagram from left to right. The four boxes on the left are the four
packages you can install. Each lets you write in its own language, and all four
produce the same specification. It travels as plain text to `gog-cli`, a small
program whose only job is to carry it across.

From there it reaches `gog-core`, and that is where all of the real work
happens: choosing the axes, the tick marks, the colors, the spacing, and the
position of every dot on the page. What comes out at the far end is the picture.

Two things follow from that shape, and the second one matters more.

The first is that a plot is text. You can save it, mail it to someone, keep it
in a file beside your data, or write a program that produces one. In most
libraries a plot is a live thing inside your session, and none of that is easy.

The second is that the four packages do no drawing. Not one of them decides
where a single dot goes. There is nothing inside them that could disagree,
because there is nothing inside them that makes that kind of decision.

## The four sentences

Here is the same plot in each language.

```r
# R
data(gm) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + color(continent)
```

```python
# Python
data(gm) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + color(col.continent)
```

```julia
# Julia
data(gm) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + color(:continent)
```

The first three are one sentence three times. They differ only in how a column
is named: a bare word in R, `col.gdp` in Python, `:gdp` in Julia. That is the
host language's business and not the grammar's.

JavaScript is the one exception, and the reason is the language itself:

```js
// JavaScript
plot(data(gm), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life), color(col.continent))
```

JavaScript cannot give `+`, `*`, `|` or `/` a meaning on objects. Whatever you
put on either side, `a + b` is a number and `a | b` is a bitwise integer. There
is no version of the language in which `data(gm) + point` builds a plot.

So each operator becomes a word:

| In the other three | What it does | In JavaScript |
|---|---|---|
| `+` | adds one atom to a plot | the comma inside `plot(...)` |
| `*` | derives one atom from another | `layer(...)` |
| <code>&#124;</code> | splits a plot into panel columns | `across(...)` |
| `/` | splits a plot into panel rows | `down(...)` |
| <code>&#124;</code> | sets two plots side by side | `beside(...)` |
| `/` | puts one plot under another | `below(...)` |

Six words for four operators, and the last four rows are the reason. In the
other three languages `|` means two different things, and you tell them apart by
what comes after it: either a way of splitting one plot into panels, or a second
plot to sit beside the first. An operator can mean both. A word cannot, so each
meaning needs a word of its own.

That is the real cost of the missing operators, and it is a cost in vocabulary
rather than in what you can draw. Everything above is still the same grammar,
and GOG's [book](https://psychometrician.github.io/gog-book/) gives it
[a chapter of its own](https://psychometrician.github.io/gog-book/bindings/javascript.html)
rather than pretending the binding is identical.

## How all four are kept the same

Not by hoping. That book has 59 chapters, and every plot in it is
drawn by the engine as the page builds rather than saved as a picture. So the
book is also a list of every plot the grammar can make.

Every time the code changes, that list is pulled out of the book and drawn again
from Python, from JavaScript and from Julia. Each result is compared against the
one R produced. Nothing is sampled and nothing is skipped.

That is **741 specifications**, drawn three more times each, on every change.
If one of the four stops matching, the check names the exact plot that came out
different.
You get a file to open rather than a vague worry.

One release was stopped before it shipped, and the reason is worth telling.

All four bindings had drawn the same scatterplot. The four pictures looked the
same. Anyone looking at the four pictures would have said they were finished.

But a plot here is a text file, in the way a web page is. It is a list of
instructions: draw a line from here to here, put this label at this spot. So the
test never compares pictures. It compares files.

R's file was one character shorter than the other three. One number in it had
been written out slightly differently.

Nobody would have found that by looking at the plots. The test found it in
seconds, and the release waited until it was fixed.

## The engine ships twice

The static picture comes from a compiled binary. But a plot on a web page can
turn under the mouse, and that needs the engine in the browser, so `gog-core`
is also compiled to WebAssembly.

There is no `wasm-bindgen`. The whole interface is three C functions over a byte
buffer, and the JavaScript side of it is about thirty lines. That was a
deliberate choice. The generated glue would have saved some of those thirty
lines, and it would have added a dependency. This project has almost none, and
keeping it that way was worth more than the lines.

It comes to 811 KB, or about 291 KB once compressed. That is with the build
tuned for size rather than speed: `opt-level = "z"`, link-time optimization, a
single codegen unit, `panic = "abort"`, and the symbols stripped.

Add a third position and the plot stands up off the page. Drag it:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + z(population) + color(continent)
```

It is the same text the command line engine reads. The browser hands it over in
memory rather than through a pipe, and the same Rust code draws it.

## The controls need no engine

Look under any plot on this page, including the flat scatterplot at the top.
There is a row of five small boxes: zoom out, zoom in, fit the whole picture, a
label telling you the plot can be dragged, and a camera that saves what you are
looking at as an image file. A box is dimmed when there is nothing for it to do.

None of that touches the engine. Those five come from 23 KB of JavaScript that
never loads WebAssembly at all, because zooming and panning and saving are done
by moving the picture you already have. The 811 KB engine is fetched only by the
plots that genuinely cannot manage without it, which is the cube above and any
plot with a selection on it. A page of ordinary plots never asks for it.

That split is worth stating plainly, because it is not what usually happens. In
most libraries a finished plot is a still image. To zoom into it, or to save a
larger copy, you move to a different package, and that package is usually much
heavier, because it is built around a live widget rather than a picture.

Here the still picture keeps its controls, and a reader pays for the engine only
on the plots that use it.

## What this is not

It is version 0.0.3, and that number is accurate. The project is young, there
are things mature libraries draw that it cannot, and the book keeps a dated list
of exactly what those are.

The checks above also prove less than they appear to. They prove the four
packages agree with each other. They cannot prove that all four are right. A box
whose whiskers reached the wrong value would pass every one of them, four times
over, and the book would print it as though it were correct.

## What you can do

### Read the book

It is [live](https://psychometrician.github.io/gog-book/): 654 plots, every one
drawn by the engine as the page builds, not a single screenshot. The
[JavaScript chapter](https://psychometrician.github.io/gog-book/bindings/javascript.html)
covers the operator problem above in full.

### Install it

Three of the four bindings carry the engine inside the package, built for your
platform, so there is no toolchain to set up.

```r
# R
install.packages("gog", repos = c("https://psychometrician.r-universe.dev",
                                  "https://cloud.r-project.org"))
```

```bash
# Python
pip install gog
```

```julia
# Julia
using Pkg; Pkg.add("GrammarOfGraphics")
```

```bash
# JavaScript
npm install grammar-of-graphics
```

### Try to make two of them disagree

Write the same specification in two of the four languages, save both, and
compare the files. If they differ by so much as one character, that is a bug worth more to
this project than any feature request, and
[the issues are open](https://github.com/psychometrician/gog/issues).

### Check a plot against a tool you trust

Same reasoning as above: agreement between four bindings is not correctness.
Draw data you know well here and in something you already believe, and tell us
where the two differ.

The [source is on GitHub](https://github.com/psychometrician/gog), Apache 2.0.

Be agog. Use gog.
